title: {{NAME}} and the Court of Fallen Lights
moral: When you listen to the voice that has been silenced, you often find the truth that changes everything.

pages.content: The fairy realm of Lumenwild existed in the space between one heartbeat and the next, tucked inside a great hollow oak at the edge of the Mirewood forest, and {{NAME}} had stumbled into it by following a trail of silver moths on a Tuesday evening. The realm was magnificent in the way that only places outside of ordinary time can be, all spiralling towers of amber resin, bridges of woven moongrass, and lanterns that burned with light caught from distant stars. But something was wrong. The lanterns, {{NAME}} noticed immediately, were going out. One by one, across the soaring canopy of the realm, lights that had burned since before any living fairy could remember were simply winking out, leaving spreading patches of cold grey darkness where warmth had always lived. The Fairy Court was in uproar. Queen Thessaly paced her dais in a gown of beaten gold, her wings furled tight against her back in the way wings go when their owner is truly frightened.

pages.content: Lord Caspiel, the Queen's chief advisor, had an explanation already prepared, the way people with explanations always do. He stood before the court with his iridescent wings fanned wide and his voice carrying with practiced authority, declaring that the lights were dying because of an old curse laid by a rival clan, the Thornwings, who lived in the gnarled roots below. The assembled fairies murmured and bristled, and {{NAME}} watched as their faces hardened with the particular expression of people who have chosen to believe something before examining it carefully. But near the back of the court, almost invisible in the shadows, a small fairy sat absolutely still. She was young, her wings no larger than autumn leaves, her expression not angry or frightened but profoundly, carefully sad. {{NAME}} made his way through the buzzing crowd and crouched beside her. Her name, she whispered, was Wren, and she had been trying to tell someone for three days what she believed was actually happening, but no one in the court thought it worth listening to a junior lamplighter.

pages.content: Wren's theory was this: the lanterns of Lumenwild were not lit by magic but by a living network of luminous root-threads, thin as silk and long as rivers, that ran through the walls and floors of the whole realm. She had tended them her whole life. Something had broken the deepest root-thread, the source thread, far below in the caverns beneath the oak, and unless it was repaired, every light in the realm would go out before morning. She could not fix it alone. She needed someone without wings, someone who could climb down the root-shafts that were too narrow for any fairy to navigate. She needed {{NAME}}. They moved fast. Wren led him behind the court, through a crack in the amber wall, down a twisting passage that descended steeply into warmth and darkness. {{NAME}} climbed hand over hand down root-shafts that were exactly as narrow and exactly as far down as he had hoped they would not be, with Wren's small bright light bobbing below him like a guide star, her voice calm and precise with directions.

pages.content: The source thread, when they found it, had been pinched and slowly strangled by the growth of a great mineral crystal that had pushed through the cavern wall over centuries, pressing against the luminous root with the patient, indifferent force of stone. It was nobody's fault and nobody's curse. {{NAME}} worked carefully, wedging a fragment of loose root-bark behind the crystal to ease its pressure, millimetre by careful millimetre, Wren watching with her wings held perfectly still and her whole small self trembling with the enormity of the moment. Then, with a sound like a single musical note played by an instrument no one had ever named, the light returned. It flooded upward through every thread, every passage, every wall, racing through the realm like dawn accelerating a thousand times over, and from far above they heard the fairy court erupt in a sound that was half cry and half song. Wren turned to {{NAME}} in the now brilliantly lit cavern, and her face was incandescent with a joy too large for her small frame to hold comfortably.

pages.content: Queen Thessaly met them at the top of the root-shaft with the entire court assembled behind her, and the silence before she spoke was the kind that holds something important. She thanked Wren first, then {{NAME}}, and then she looked at Lord Caspiel for a long moment without saying anything at all, which seemed to be sufficient. Wren was given a new title and a lantern of her own, one that burned with the particular warm gold of the source thread, and she held it as if it weighed more than the whole world. {{NAME}} was escorted back through the hollow oak and out into the Mirewood as the first true dark of evening fell, every lantern of Lumenwild blazing behind him through the gaps in the bark. He walked home through the trees feeling warm and full of something he couldn't quite name, the kind of satisfied tiredness that comes only from doing something that mattered. The silver moths drifted around him like small friendly stars, and his footsteps slowed, and the soft forest dark settled over him like a blanket, and just before he reached the edge of the wood he heard, very faintly, what sounded like a tiny voice calling his name from somewhere deep among the roots.
